Cite the paper and page from the passage, and read the PDF page before relying on a claim.
notes: CORE bundles several findings (DoT definition, MAD on two tasks, GPT-3.5-Turbo+MAD over GPT-4 on Common MT, adaptive break, tit-for-tat level, judge self-preference); it is graded by its empirical parts. RES-COMMONMT: 'significant advancements' has no reported test, and the extracted Table 1 gives GPT-4 and GPT-3.5-Turbo+MAD the same Lexical COMET (82.0, p5 L29 and L57). RES-DOT-MITIGATION: the record's quote holds only the table numbers (the 'Table 4: Mitigation of Degeneration-of-Thought' caption is at p6 L81), and its setting names GPT-3.5-Turbo, which the Section 4.1 passages do not state. RES-WEAK-JUDGE: the quote stops mid-sentence ('plays a secondary'); the outcome is translation quality, not judge accuracy. RES-JUDGE-BIAS: the dataset behind Table 6 is not named; each row's counts sum to 200, which is not the 1000-example Common MT test set that Section 4 names as its default. The record text treats the negative side's role as a finding, while the paper states it as a belief. RES-TIT-FOR-TAT: the record's setting names GPT-3.5-Turbo, which the passages do not state. LIM-1's quote stops before its final words ('distinct LLMs.', p9 L33). No result in this paper reports a confidence interval, standard error or significance test.

method.description: Zero-shot experiments compare MAD (an affirmative and a negative LLM debater plus an LLM judge that can end the debate early) with single-model baselines and Self-Reflect on Common MT and Counter-Intuitive AR, followed by analyses such as forcing the judge to stop at a fixed debate iteration.

passages.text:
We conducted experiments on both natural language generation and understanding through two
challenging tasks, namely, Commonsense Machine

Translation (Common MT) and Counter-Intuitive
Arithmetic Reasoning (Counter-Intuitive AR). The
common characteristic of the two tasks is that our
instincts are mostly incorrect based on only the superficial expressions of the questions, and deeper
levels of contemplation are required for better answers. Experimental results demonstrate that our
MAD framework outperforms the baseline methods, especially, GPT-3.5-Turbo with MAD can
surpass the performance of GPT-4 on Common MT.

The debate has no stopping rule other than a maximum of 3 iterations; the judge may stop it early (adaptive break) when it believes the best answer has been reached.
The surpass-GPT-4 finding is stated for MAD with GPT-3.5-Turbo as backbone on the Common MT dataset.

method.description: Self-Reflect and MAD are compared on bias (a human-evaluated rate of ambiguity errors in the translations) and on diversity (100 minus the Self-BLEU between the initial translation and the revised or negative-side translation), reported in Table 4.

passages.text:
• Bias: We observe that LLMs often rely on direct
intuition, which can lead to incorrect or inappropriate responses. To address this problem, we
use human evaluation to determine the ambiguity
error rate of LLMs’ responses, examining if the
LLM’s output is biased.
• Diversity: LLMs are resistant to changing their
answers and lack diverse reflection. The diversity of the translations is evaluated using the
Self-BLEU score (Yin et al., 2020). In other
words, methods lacking diverse reflection produce more similar translation candidates. Consequently, higher Self-BLEU scores mean lower
diversity. We calculate text diversity via:
Diversity = 100 − Self_BLEU (Cand1 , Cand2 ) (2)

In formula (2), candidates 1 and 2 represent the
initial translation (base answer in Self-Reflection or
affirmative side’s response in MAD) and the current

translation (possible modified answer after SelfReflection or negative side’s response in MAD).
As shown in Table 4, Bias and Rigidity are significant factors causing DoT. In addition, addressing
these biases and stereotypes through self-reflection
can be challenging. MAD framework effectively
corrects inherent biases in translation, mitigates
DoT, and considerably improves performance.

stated_hypotheses: DoT is taken to arise from three factors (bias and distorted perception, rigidity and resistance to change, limited external feedback); MAD is said to address limited external feedback by design, and this experiment targets the first two.
Section 4 results are on the Common MT dataset unless otherwise stated.

passages.text:
As mentioned in the Section 1, the DoT problem
originates from three factors: (1) Bias and Distorted Perception, (2) Rigidity and Resistance to
Change, and (3) Limited External Feedback. In
our MAD framework, we introduce the views of
other agents in the form of debates, solving the phenomenon of limited external feedback (problem 3).
Next, this section will delve into the mitigation of
problems 1 and 2 through experiments.

In this section, we present a qualitative analysis to
provide some insights how MAD works. Unless
otherwise stated, we report the overall results on
the Common MT dataset.
